ABSTRACT: The installation of fluorine and fluorinated functional groups into drug-like scaffolds can perturb the physicochemical,
pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic properties of compounds. However, some potentially useful fluorinated substructures reside
predominantly outside the realm of the current synthetic methodologies. One such substructure, the α,α-difluorophosphine oxide,
might be convergently prepared by the reaction of a gem-difluorinated alkene with a P−H bond, though such nucleophilic reactions
instead proceed through a C−F substitution pathway that delivers monofluorovinyl products. In contrast, we report a peroxide-
initiated hydrophosphinylation reaction of gem-difluoroalkenes that avoids C−F substitution and produces a wide range of α,α-
difluorophosphine oxides and functions using readily available reagents and green solvents.
■INTRODUCTION
The incorporation of fluorine and fluorinated functional
groups into organic molecules has become a staple in modern
synthetic organic chemistry,1−3 as the presence of one or more
fluorine atoms in a molecule can significantly alter
physicochemical properties that are important for the design
of therapeutics, biological probes, agrichemicals, and materials.
Similarly, phosphorus containing functional groups are also
prominent in the pharmaceutical and agricultural industries,
with phosphates, phosphonates, and phosphoramidates widely
employed.4,5 Moreover, the combination of these groups
provides α-fluorophosphates and α,α-difluorophosphonates
that have special uses in medicinal chemistry and chemical
biology as metabolically stabile phosphate mimics.6
In contrast, phosphine oxides are a common phosphorus-
containing functional group that typically impart polarity into a
molecule and also improve the aqueous solubility and
metabolic stability at the cost of membrane permeability,4
though the corresponding α,α-difluorophosphine oxides
(CF2−P(O)R2) have been less studied, and generalized
methods to deliver α,α-difluorophosphine oxides have not
been developed.4 The available strategies involve perfluor-
oalkylation using stoichiometric Sn-based reagents (Figure
1A),7 rely on a nucleophilic “P−CF2
−” precursor (Figure 1B),8
or use a tailored hypervalent iodine reagent (Figure 1C),9
which combined require specialized reagents, only react with a
limited scope of benzaldehyde electrophiles, and/or only react
with a limited substrate scope of fluoroalkanes.
As a complementary strategy for accessing α,α-difluoro-
phosphine oxides, retrosynthetic disconnection of the C−P
bond might reveal an electrophilic gem-difluoroalkene and a
nucleophilic phosphine oxide (Figure 2A). The gem-difluor-
oalkene, bearing an electrophilic character at the terminal
difluorinated carbon atom,10 represents an attractive electro-
phile for nucleophilic addition. However, nucleophilic addition
reactions of gem-difluoroalkenes with a wide variety of
nucleophiles that proceed under basic conditions typically
generate anionic intermediates that decompose through β−F
elimination to deliver monofluorinated products,11−14 which is
generally true for reactions of P-based nucleophiles (Figure

In contrast, the addition of P-based radicals into gem-
difluoroalkenes avoids the pitfalls of nucleophilic addition/
elimination sequences (Figure 2D).17 This radical-based
strategy has proved useful in hydrothiolation reactions of
aliphatic gem-difluorinated alkenes to generate new C−S
bonds18 and hydrophosphinylation reactions of unactivated
alkenes to generate new C−P bonds.19 However, for gem-
difluoroalkenes, only a single example exists of a corresponding
hydrophosphinylation reaction of a dialkyl-substituted gem-
difluoroalkene to generate an α,α-difluorodiphenylphosphine
oxide, which uses an uncommon peroxide to initiate the radical
chain process, and generates a mixture of regioisomers (Figure
2D).17 Moreover, this process requires the use of two charges
of the peroxide initiator and has not been extrapolated to
reactions of styrenyl alkenes, electronically perturbed diary-
lphosphine oxides, and dialkylphosphine oxides. To circum-
vent previous limitations, we report a hydrophosphinylation
reaction to convert a broad spectrum of gem-difluoroalkenes to
α,α-difluorophosphine oxides using a single charge of readily
available peroxide initiator with complete regioselectivity for
the gem-difluorinated position (Figure 2E).
■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Taking inspiration from Piettre17,20 and Kovensky,21 gem-
difluorostyrene 1a was reacted with diphenylphosphine oxide
(2a) in the presence of 0.5 equiv of di-tert-butyl peroxide in
tert-butanol at 120 °C for 16 h to yield hydrophosphinylated
product 3a in 82% yield (Table 1, entry 1). Because the
peroxide decomposed upon heating above 100 °C, we first
explored varying the amount of di-tert-butyl peroxide (entries
2−7). However, increasing the amount of peroxide resulted in
nonproductive conversion (entries 2−4). The use of
decreasing quantities of peroxide improved the conversion of
1a, with the use of 5% di-tert-butyl peroxide providing the best
yield (entry 7). Increasing the equivalents of diphenylphos-
phine oxide to three provided a quantitative yield of the
corresponding product, while the use of 4 equiv afforded a
lower yield of product (entries 8−9). For this system, DMF
and tBuOH typically performed best, with reactions conducted
in other solvents, such as nitromethane and butyronitrile, did
not generate the product (entries 8, 10−12 and Table S1).
Moreover, the use of tBuOH provides a greener alternative22,23
relative to prior works that required the use of benzene.17,21
The optimized reaction conditions enabled coupling of a
wide array of gem-difluoroalkenes with diphenylphosphine
oxide to deliver difluorinated products exclusively (Figure 3).
In general, for a new substrate combination, the reactions were
scouted in both tBuOH and DMF on a small scale (0.1 mmol),
and the better-performing reaction was repeated on a larger
(1.0 mmol) scale. Electron-rich difluorostyrenes containing
ethers, thioethers, and alkyl groups reacted smoothly, giving
moderate to excellent yields (3a−3g; 56−90%). Electron-
deficient difluorostyrenes containing O-benzyl, biphenyl,
phenyl ester, trifluoromethyl, nitrile, tosyl, diethylamide, and
methyl ester were also tolerated, and the corresponding
products were isolated in good to excellent yields (3h−3o;
62−96%). gem-Difluorostyrenes bearing halogen atoms also
reacted to give the corresponding α,α-difluorophosphine
oxides in moderate to excellent yields (3p−3r; 58−89%).
Substrates containing heterocyclic scaffolds including dibenzo-
thiophene, pyrazole, and a benzenesulfonyl-protected indole
were compatible with this system (3s−3u; 60−83%).
Furthermore, two alkyl-derived gem-difluoroalkenes reacted
smoothly under the standard reaction conditions with
complete regioselectivity at the difluorinated position (3v−
3w; 65−72%), in contrast to a previously published work that

However, alkyl-trisubstituted gem-difluoroalkenes only pro-

A series of distinct phosphorus nucleophiles were coupled
with gem-difluorostyrene 1a to deliver a series of α,α-
difluorophosphine oxides (Figure 4). Diarylphosphines bearing
electron-donating 3,5-dimethyl, 4-methoxy, 4-methyl groups,
and electron-withdrawing 3-trifluoromethyl groups reacted
smoothly to deliver α,α-difluorophosphine oxides (4a−4d;
73−84%). Additionally, ethyl phenyl phosphinate [HP(O)-
(OEt)Ph] reacted with 1a and 20% di-tert-butyl peroxide,
albeit in a diminished yield (4e; 29%). Furthermore, di-n-
pentyl phosphine oxide provided the hydrophosphinylation
product in a useful yield (4f; 50%), which represents the first
example of a reaction of a dialkylphosphine oxide nucleo-
phile.17,20,21 However, diethyl phosphite [HP(O)(OEt)2] did
not react under these reaction conditions and further attempts
to optimize the conditions (time, solvent, temperature, other
peroxides) were unsuccessful (4g, trace).
Based on the literature precedent and physicochemical data,
we propose that the hydrophosphinylation reaction proceeds
by a free-radical chain mechanism (Scheme 1). Initial thermal
decomposition of the peroxide generates
•OtBu 5, which
undergoes β-scission to generate •CH3 (6) and acetone,24 the
latter of which was detected as a stoichiometric byproduct by
GCMS in standard reactions. Next,
•CH3 (6) abstracts a
hydrogen atom from diphenylphosphine oxide (P−H bond
dissociation energy = 83.3 kcal/mol)25 to generate CH4 (C−H
bond dissociation energy = 104.8 kcal/mol),26 followed by
regioselective addition of P-centered radical 2a′ to the
difluorinated position of the gem-difluoroalkene (1) to give
carbon-centered radical intermediate 7.27 The radical inter-
mediate (7) then abstracts H• from an equivalent of
diphenylphosphine oxide to deliver the final product and
propagate the phosphorus-centered radical 2a′ for further
iterations of the sequence.19,27 Of note, the poor reactivity of
alkyl-trisubstituted gem-difluoroalkenes likely arises from the
poor radical stability of the carbon-centered radical inter-
mediate, as compared to the corresponding benzylic-stabilized
gem-difluorostyrenes or the tetra-substituted alkyl gem-
difluoroalkenes.
■CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, a hydrophosphinylation reaction that employs a
readily available peroxide catalyst adds diaryl and dialkyl
phosphine oxides across a broad spectrum of gem-difluor-
oalkenes to generate α,α-difluorophosphine oxides. By
exploiting a radical-based mechanism, the process avoids
anionic intermediates that promote the loss of fluoride.
Relative to prior works, beneficial features of this system
involve use of a commercially available catalyst, a single charge
of reagents, and a green solvent (tBuOH). Ongoing work to
develop complementary hydrofunctionalization reactions of
fluorinated alkenes will be reported in due time.
